summary: The Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 representing accrued interest on the assessee 's money lending investments. The Wealth Tax Officer deleted the additions of Rs.1,50,00, representing accrued interest. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and contended that accrued interest was liable to be included in the wealth tax assessments of the assessee. The Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Orissa, dismissed the appeals. The Commissioner held that accrued interest could not be included in wealth tax assessments. The Commissioner also held that accrued interests were liable to be excluded in the wealth of the assessee '. The Commissioner, however, deleted the additions. The assessee preferred an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal dismissed the appeal. The Revenue appealed to the Tribunal. The assessee contended that the decision of the Tribunal was contrary to the decision of this Court in Vedreva Venkappa Rao vs Commissioner of Wealth tax, Orissa, and Orissa vs Vysyaraju Badreenarayana Moorthy Raju (Orissa)(1) and Orissa vs Commissioner of Income tax, Orissa and Orissa vs Orissa vs V.ysyaraju, Badreen Narayana Moorthy Raju and Orissa vs Income Tax Officer, Orissa and others, and that the decision was contrary to law. The Tribunal held that the decision in Vedrevam Venkappa Rao was not binding on the Revenue and that the judgment of the Orissa High Court was binding on the revenue. The Tribunal also held that the judgment in Vedreya Venkappa Rao 's case was not binding. The Tribunal, however, held that the assessee ' was entitled to be included as a " wealth tax officer in the wealth ' assessment of the assessee and that the assessee was entitled to the benefit of the said decision. The Tribunal allowed the appeal and held that the Tribunal was right in holding that the assessee had not been included in the Wealth Tax assessment. The Tribunal further held that the appellant was entitled to claim the benefit of section 10(1)(a) of the Wealth Tax Act, 1957 and that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the Tribunal 's decision was contrary in law and that the High Court was in error in holding that it was not open to the Revenue to question the validity of the decision of a Tribunal. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Tribunal was right and in law
